ls: `ls` lists files and directories in the current working directory. Common flags: `-l` long format, `-a` include hidden, `-h` human-readable sizes, `-t` sort by modification time.
ssh: SSH (Secure Shell) is a protocol and command for securely logging into a remote system over an encrypted channel. Typical use: `ssh user@host`.
hostname: `hostname` displays or sets the system's host name. In sessions it identifies which server you are connected to.
date: `date` displays or sets the system date and time. Commonly used to verify server clock and session timing.
whoami: `whoami` prints the effective username of the current user.
pwd: `pwd` prints the current working directory path.
sudo: `sudo` runs a command with elevated (root) privileges. It is a high-risk command in production environments. Flags: `-n` non-interactive, `-i` login shell as root, `-u` run as a specific user.
chmod: `chmod` changes file or directory permissions. `+x` adds execute, `777` gives read/write/execute to everyone (world-writable, high-risk), `600` restricts to owner.
chown: `chown` changes file or directory ownership. Example: `chown user:group file`.
chgrp: `chgrp` changes the group ownership of a file or directory.
cat: `cat` concatenates and prints file contents to standard output.
grep: `grep` searches for text patterns inside files or piped input. Common flags: `-i` case-insensitive, `-r` recursive, `-n` line numbers, `-v` invert match, `-E` extended regex.
egrep: `egrep` is grep with extended regular expressions, equivalent to `grep -E`.
fgrep: `fgrep` searches for fixed strings without regex interpretation, equivalent to `grep -F`.
cd: `cd` changes the current working directory. `cd -` returns to the previous directory, `cd ~` goes home.
mkdir: `mkdir` creates a new directory. `-p` creates parents as needed.
rm: `rm` removes files or directories. `-r` recursive, `-f` force, `-i` prompt. `rm -rf` is destructive and high-risk.
cp: `cp` copies files and directories. `-r` recursive, `-p` preserve attributes, `-a` archive (preserve everything).
mv: `mv` moves or renames files and directories.
ln: `ln` creates links between files. `-s` creates a symbolic (soft) link.
touch: `touch` creates an empty file or updates the modification time of an existing file.
stat: `stat` shows detailed file metadata: size, permissions, timestamps, inode.
file: `file` classifies files by inspecting their content (e.g., ELF binary, ASCII text, JPEG image).
readlink: `readlink` prints the target of a symbolic link.
basename: `basename` strips directory and suffix from a path, leaving just the filename.
dirname: `dirname` strips the trailing filename from a path, leaving just the directory portion.
passwd: `passwd` changes user passwords. Treated as a credential operation and audited closely.
useradd: `useradd` creates a new user account. Requires root and is a high-value action.
userdel: `userdel` removes a user account. `-r` also removes the home directory.
usermod: `usermod` modifies an existing user account (groups, shell, home, etc.).
history: `history` shows previously executed shell commands. `-c` clears history and is an anti-forensics risk. `-w` writes it to disk.
echo: `echo` prints text to standard output or redirects it to files.
printf: `printf` prints formatted output; a more precise alternative to `echo`.
curl: `curl` transfers data from or to a server over HTTP(S), FTP, and other protocols. Flags: `-X` HTTP method, `-o` write to file, `-H` header, `-d` data. Piping curl to a shell is high-risk.
wget: `wget` downloads files from the network. `-c` resume, `-r` recursive, `-O` output filename.
scp: `scp` securely copies files between hosts over SSH. `-r` recursive, `-i` identity key, `-P` port. Can exfiltrate data — flagged as network transfer activity.
rsync: `rsync` synchronizes files locally or over the network. `-a` archive, `-z` compress, `-v` verbose, `--delete` remove extra files. Remote rsync can move large volumes.
sftp: `sftp` is an interactive secure file transfer program that runs over SSH.
ftp: `ftp` is a plaintext file transfer client — legacy and insecure; not recommended in production.
telnet: `telnet` is a plaintext remote-shell client — legacy and insecure. Sometimes used to test TCP ports.
nc: `nc` (netcat) reads and writes data across network connections. Used for port scanning, banner grabs, ad hoc listeners, and reverse shells.
netcat: `netcat` reads and writes data across network connections. Same tool as `nc`. Frequently misused for reverse shells.
ncat: `ncat` is the Nmap project's netcat replacement, with TLS and IPv6 support.
socat: `socat` is a bidirectional data relay — like netcat but far more flexible.
ping: `ping` sends ICMP echo requests to test reachability and measure round-trip time.
traceroute: `traceroute` shows the network path (hops) taken to reach a host.
tracepath: `tracepath` is a simpler traceroute that does not require root.
mtr: `mtr` combines ping and traceroute into a live network diagnostic.
nslookup: `nslookup` queries DNS servers for name resolution information.
host: `host` is a lightweight DNS lookup utility.
ip: `ip` is the modern Linux networking tool. `ip a` shows addresses, `ip r` shows routes, `ip link` shows interfaces.
ifconfig: `ifconfig` is the legacy tool for viewing/configuring network interfaces, replaced by `ip`.
route: `route` shows or manipulates the IP routing table (legacy; use `ip r`).
arp: `arp` shows the ARP cache mapping IP addresses to MAC addresses.
su: `su` switches the effective user. `su -` starts a full login shell as the target user. Common privilege-escalation vector.
ps: `ps` reports a snapshot of running processes. `ps aux` shows all processes for all users; `ps -ef` shows every process with parent PID.
top: `top` displays live CPU and memory usage for running processes.
htop: `htop` is an interactive, colorful replacement for `top`.
iotop: `iotop` shows real-time disk I/O usage per process (requires root).
iftop: `iftop` shows real-time bandwidth usage per connection.
vmstat: `vmstat` reports virtual memory, CPU, and I/O statistics.
iostat: `iostat` reports CPU and disk I/O statistics.
free: `free` shows total, used, and free memory. `-h` for human-readable.
uptime: `uptime` shows how long the system has been running plus load averages.
w: `w` shows who is logged in and what they are doing.
id: `id` prints user and group identity information for the current or specified user.
groups: `groups` prints group memberships for a user.
kill: `kill` sends signals to processes. `-9` (SIGKILL) forcefully terminates; `-15` (SIGTERM) requests graceful shutdown.
killall: `killall` sends a signal to processes by name rather than PID.
pkill: `pkill` kills processes matching a pattern (name, user, terminal, etc.).
pgrep: `pgrep` lists PIDs of processes matching a pattern.
find: `find` searches the filesystem for files matching criteria. `-name` by name, `-type f/d` by type, `-exec` run a command per match. Often used in reconnaissance.
locate: `locate` uses a prebuilt database to find files quickly (updated by `updatedb`).
which: `which` shows the full path of an executable in the current `PATH`.
whereis: `whereis` locates binaries, sources, and manuals for a command.
type: `type` tells you whether a name is a shell builtin, alias, function, or file.
tail: `tail` shows the last lines of a file. `-f` follows new writes; `-n N` shows the last N lines.
head: `head` shows the first lines of a file. `-n N` for the first N lines.
less: `less` pages through file output interactively; supports search and navigation.
more: `more` pages through output one screen at a time (older/simpler than `less`).
wc: `wc` counts lines, words, and bytes in files. `-l` lines only.
sort: `sort` sorts lines of text. `-n` numeric, `-r` reverse, `-u` unique.
uniq: `uniq` collapses adjacent duplicate lines. Usually piped after `sort`.
cut: `cut` extracts columns from lines. `-d ':' -f 1` splits on `:` and returns the first field.
tr: `tr` translates or deletes characters from standard input.
tee: `tee` duplicates standard input to standard output and to files.
xargs: `xargs` builds and executes command lines from standard input (useful with `find ... | xargs cmd`).
sed: `sed` is a stream editor for text transformation. Example: `sed 's/old/new/g' file` replaces all occurrences.
awk: `awk` is a pattern-scanning and text-processing language. Example: `awk '{print $1}'` prints the first field of each line.
vi: `vi`/`vim` is a powerful modal terminal text editor.
vim: `vim` is an improved version of vi, the standard terminal text editor.
nano: `nano` is a simple, beginner-friendly terminal text editor.
emacs: `emacs` is an extensible text editor and integrated environment.
tar: `tar` archives files. `-c` create, `-x` extract, `-t` list, `-v` verbose, `-f` file, `-z` gzip, `-j` bzip2. Combined with remote transfer, can package data for exfiltration.
gzip: `gzip` compresses a file to `.gz` in place. `gunzip` or `gzip -d` decompresses.
bzip2: `bzip2` compresses files with better ratio than gzip. `bunzip2` decompresses.
xz: `xz` is a high-ratio compressor producing `.xz` files.
df: `df` reports filesystem disk space usage. `-h` human-readable.
du: `du` estimates disk usage of files and directories. `-sh` gives a summary in human-readable form.
mount: `mount` attaches a filesystem to the directory tree. Requires root for most mounts.
lsblk: `lsblk` lists block devices (disks and partitions) in a tree.
blkid: `blkid` prints block-device attributes such as UUID and filesystem type.
fdisk: `fdisk` manipulates disk partition tables (destructive; root required).
parted: `parted` is an advanced partition editor supporting GPT.
mkfs: `mkfs` creates a filesystem on a block device (e.g., `mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1`). Destructive.
service: `service` is the legacy wrapper to start/stop init.d services (largely superseded by systemctl).
journalctl: `journalctl` queries the systemd journal for service and kernel logs. `-u <service>` filters by unit; `-f` follows live.
dmesg: `dmesg` prints kernel ring-buffer messages (hardware, drivers, boot).
crontab: `crontab` edits scheduled jobs for a user. Unauthorized cron entries can establish persistence. `crontab -l` lists, `crontab -e` edits.
cron: `cron` is the scheduler daemon that runs jobs defined in crontabs.
at: `at` schedules a one-off command to run at a future time.
iptables: `iptables` configures the legacy Linux firewall. Rules are per-chain (INPUT/OUTPUT/FORWARD).
nft: `nft` (nftables) is the modern replacement for iptables.
ufw: `ufw` (Uncomplicated Firewall) is a user-friendly wrapper over iptables/nftables on Ubuntu.
firewalld: `firewalld` is the RHEL/Fedora dynamic firewall manager using zones.
netstat: `netstat` prints network connections, routing tables, and interface statistics (legacy).
ss: `ss` is the modern replacement for netstat. `ss -tulpen` shows listening TCP/UDP sockets with owning processes.
lsof: `lsof` lists open files and the processes that opened them. Useful for finding what's using a port or file.
env: `env` prints environment variables or runs a command with a modified environment.
export: `export` sets shell environment variables for child processes.
unset: `unset` removes a shell variable or function.
source: `source` (or `.`) executes commands from a file in the current shell.
bash: `bash` is the Bourne-again shell. Runs interactively or executes scripts.
sh: `sh` runs commands in the POSIX shell (often a symlink to bash or dash).
zsh: `zsh` is an extended Unix shell with rich completion and plugins.
python: `python` runs Python code. May be used for scripting, tooling, or reverse shells by attackers.
perl: `perl` is a text-processing language often available on servers.
node: `node` runs JavaScript with the Node.js runtime.
docker: `docker` manages containers. Common: `docker ps` list, `docker run` start, `docker exec` inside a container, `docker logs` view logs. Privileged containers can compromise the host.
podman: `podman` is a daemonless container engine compatible with Docker commands.
kubectl: `kubectl` controls Kubernetes clusters. `get` list, `describe` details, `apply` apply YAML, `delete` remove, `logs` container logs, `exec` run a shell in a pod.
helm: `helm` is a Kubernetes package manager for installing/upgrading application charts.
apt: `apt` installs, upgrades, or removes packages on Debian/Ubuntu. `install`, `update`, `upgrade`, `remove`.
apt-get: `apt-get` is the older, script-friendly Debian/Ubuntu package tool.
dpkg: `dpkg` is the low-level Debian package installer. `-i` install, `-r` remove.
yum: `yum` installs or removes packages on RHEL/CentOS.
dnf: `dnf` is the modern package manager on Fedora and RHEL 8+.
rpm: `rpm` is the low-level RHEL package tool.
pacman: `pacman` is the Arch Linux package manager.
brew: `brew` (Homebrew) is a popular package manager for macOS and Linux.
pip: `pip` installs Python packages, typically from PyPI.
yarn: `yarn` is an alternative Node.js package manager.
nmap: `nmap` scans hosts and ports for discovery and version detection. Common in reconnaissance and security testing.
tcpdump: `tcpdump` captures and prints network packets. Can expose sensitive traffic.
wireshark: `wireshark` (or `tshark`) captures and analyzes network packets with a rich decoder.
openssl: `openssl` handles TLS/SSL certificates, keys, hashes, and general cryptographic operations.
gpg: `gpg` is the GNU Privacy Guard tool for signing, encrypting, and managing PGP keys.
ssh-keygen: `ssh-keygen` generates and manages SSH key pairs used for authentication.
ssh-copy-id: `ssh-copy-id` installs a public key onto a remote host for passwordless SSH login.
ssh-agent: `ssh-agent` holds decrypted SSH private keys in memory to avoid repeated passphrase prompts.
sha256sum: `sha256sum` computes SHA-256 hashes to verify integrity of files.
md5sum: `md5sum` computes MD5 hashes (fast but cryptographically weak).
shasum: `shasum` computes SHA hashes of various sizes.
true: `true` does nothing and always exits successfully (status 0). Often used in scripts and in checks like `sudo -n true`.
false: `false` does nothing and always exits with status 1 (failure).
yes: `yes` outputs a string (default `y`) repeatedly — useful for piping into commands that need confirmations.
test: `test` (or `[ ... ]`) evaluates conditional expressions and returns success/failure.
uname: `uname` prints system information. `uname -a` shows kernel, hostname, and architecture in one line.
hostnamectl: `hostnamectl` controls the system hostname and reveals related metadata.
timedatectl: `timedatectl` displays and configures system time, timezone, and NTP.
loginctl: `loginctl` controls the systemd login manager (sessions, users, seats).
modprobe: `modprobe` adds or removes kernel modules along with their dependencies.
insmod: `insmod` inserts a single kernel module (no dependency handling).
sysctl: `sysctl` reads or modifies runtime kernel parameters (like `net.ipv4.ip_forward`).
lspci: `lspci` lists PCI devices attached to the system.
lsusb: `lsusb` lists USB devices attached to the system.
dmidecode: `dmidecode` prints BIOS/hardware information from DMI tables (requires root).
chattr: `chattr` changes filesystem attributes (like `+i` immutable). Used to prevent modification, sometimes for anti-forensics.
git: `git` is the distributed version control system. Common: `clone`, `pull`, `push`, `commit`, `status`, `log`, `checkout`.
svn: `svn` (Subversion) is a centralized version control system.
dd: `dd` copies raw bytes with fine-grained control. `if=source of=dest bs=1M`. Highly destructive when pointed at devices (e.g., `of=/dev/sda`).
strace: `strace` traces system calls and signals of a process — useful for debugging low-level behavior.
ltrace: `ltrace` traces library calls of a process.
perf: `perf` is a Linux profiler for CPU performance counters, tracing, and sampling.
watch: `watch` runs a command repeatedly and shows its output (e.g., `watch -n 1 ps aux`).
time: `time` measures how long a command takes to run (real, user, sys).
